transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Springwell SRE), Tom Riley (Platform), Priya Menon (Security), Evan Ortiz (Product)

Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood Console's request archaeology / trace stitching features, focusing on request logs, error surface analysis, KV/prefix cache behaviors and fallback routing. Customer interested in how to quickly find root cause for degraded responses occurring during peak traffic and how to prove cost/latency tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Topics covered:
- Trace stitching & request archaeology terminology
- Request playback and request-level logs
- KV cache / prefix cache inspection and misses analysis
- Fallback routing and model variant rollouts
- Security / data residency concerns (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
- Proposed pilot and benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Okay, hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, um, we wanted to walk through what we call request archaeology, basically how you take a single bad user request and stitch together logs, traces, and the model runtime context to find root cause. Connor will drive the console demo.

[00:22] Aisha (Springwell): Thanks. We get spikes during batch windows and then some requests just return timeouts or gibberish. We have some SLOs that are tight and need to nail the debug flow.

[00:35] Connor (Redwood SE): Great, yeah, so quick agenda: look at the trace map, then request playback, look at KV cache hits/misses, and show fallback routing when a model variant fails. I'll start share. Sorry, screen share - give me a sec.

[01:05] Tom (Springwell): Quick Q — is this the same console you showed in the quickstart? last year? sometimes the UI labels look slightly different.

[01:15] Maya: It's the Console but we've added the 'Request Archaeology' workflow as a set of linked views: trace map, request log, token timeline, and model runtime snapshot. Sometimes the auto transcripts call it con-soul, which is, uh, amusing.

[01:37] Connor: Alright opening a sample incident. You can see the request flow map on the left, it's stitched across services — API gateway, Redwood fronting pool, and then a dedicated model pool. Notice these red hops — those are p50/p95 anomalies.

[02:05] Evan (Product): Can you show the hop that indicates the KV cache miss? that's the thing we suspect.

[02:18] Connor: Yup. If I click the red node it expands to the request-level logs. Here we have the model's KV cache introspection snapshot, it's showing prefix cache hits 14/40 for this session, and there are a couple of cold-start tokens. You can download the raw dump.

[02:45] Aisha: The numbering looks off, our engineers refer to KV cache as K-V, sometimes kv — will that map to our logs?

[02:55] Connor: We normalize names but the mapping is configurable. Also note the timestamps — we've aligned trace timestamps to your API gateway time using the trace correlation id you sent. sometimes the correlation IDs are different shapes but we pick them up heuristically.

[03:27] Tom: You mentioned request playback — is that streaming the original tokens back into a sandbox model or replaying the network call?

[03:40] Connor: Good question. The playback is deterministic: we replay the original request against a pinned model snapshot in a sandbox environment, with the original prompt and tokenization. We also allow toggling kv cache state — simulate warm vs cold cache so you can see latency delta.

[04:10] Priya (Security): Where does playback run? on Redwood hosted infra, or can we run it in our VPC?

[04:20] Maya: For Hosted customers playback runs in Redwood controlled sandbox by default, but for Dedicated or Private customers we can run playback in your VPC — that’s part of the Private offering. We'll note that for the security Q&A.

[04:42] Aisha: And for the request that returned gibberish, what signals indicate model degradation vs prompt engineering problem?

[04:55] Connor: The console's output quality panel compares generated tokens against a reference evaluation set and flags hallucination patterns. For individual requests, we show token-level logits, top-k distributions and a confidence metric. In the example here you can see a sudden drop in top-1 probability around token 27.

[05:23] Evan: Are those logits accessible via API? we want to pipe them into our observability pipelines.

[05:30] Connor: Yes, there's a request-level diagnostics API that returns the same runtime snapshot: token logits, kv-cache footprint, and per-layer timing. You can stream them or pull post-hoc.

[05:50] Aisha: One of our concerns is cost — can we simulate Dedicated pool impact?

[05:58] Maya: We can. Connor will run a quick benchmark with the same workload against a Dedicated profile we have as a sample. that helps show p50/p95 improvements and estimated unit cost.

[06:20] Connor: Running the benchmark now — I'm toggling the model variant to a quantized variant and then switching to a Dedicated run. While that's running, note the trace timeline here shows a bucketed token spread, and you can inspect per-token kernel time.

[06:45] Tom: There's a note about fallback routing — if the Dedicated pool is saturated what happens? does it route to hosted and what's the data residency implication?

[06:57] Connor: We have policy-based routing. You can set route order: Dedicated -> Regional Hosted -> Lower-tier Hosted. For data residency, the route can be restricted so that only same-region hosted pools are allowed. Fallback to hosted can be encrypted in transit and we ensure logs/audit trails capture the route decision.

[07:30] Priya: For SOC2 / audit, we need to see the audit trail of fallback decisions. Is that in the console?

[07:40] Connor: Yes, the trace detail includes route decisions with timestamps and device ids. Those entries feed into the audit export. We can share a sample audit export for your compliance team.

[08:05] Aisha: About prefix cache — is that the same as KV? we've seen different terms used across the stack.

[08:18] Connor: It's related. Prefix caching stores recent prompt prefixes and their KV contents; KV refers to the cached key-value attention caches. Our UI labels both but you can toggle to see them separately. In this sample we show both prefix hits and KV buffer occupancy.

[08:50] Maya: I want to point out the anomaly detector: it surfaced that a higher-than-normal tokenization mismatch was happening, likely due to a new prompt template. That caused more cache misses.

[09:10] Evan: That sounds like an ops/prompt engineering problem — are there guardrails to prevent bad templates from rolling?

[09:20] Connor: Yes, the Console supports canary rollouts with request sampling and automatic rollback if key metrics degrade. We also have a preflight check runner that runs a prompt set against a candidate model and reports regressions.

[09:40] Tom: How granular are the canaries? can we do per-route or per-customer canaries?

[09:48] Connor: Both. Per-route, per-model, and you can tie canaries to attributes like API key, header, or user segment.

[10:05] Aisha: Let's circle back to the specific failing trace. moving to that trace, I see lots of small retries and then a time out. The request log shows 504 at the gateway after 12s.

[10:20] Connor: Right, and if you look at the model runtime snapshot we see a series of cache evictions. The KV footprint spikes right before the timeout, indicating memory pressure on that pod. There's also a p95 spike on kernel time around the same moment.

[10:45] Priya: Memory pressure — is that from larger context windows or from multiple concurrent sessions?

[10:52] Connor: In this example it's context window: a few requests sent large documents concatenated in session that exceeded our warm cache heuristics. The playback with an increased cache size reproduces the failure.

[11:20] Maya: We'll note that you can set guard rails on max context size per route, which prevents runaway contexts that cause evictions.

[11:35] Aisha: Hmm. We do occasionally allow long context for certain internal flows. Can guard rails be soft, like warn-only?

[11:44] Connor: Yes, you can have warn-only or hard-limits. Warn-only emits an alert to the console and your webhook integrations.

[12:00] Tom: On observability, can we correlate traces to our existing Datadog spans?

[12:07] Connor: Absolutely — we support trace context propagation with Datadog, X-Ray, and OpenTelemetry. We ingest your spans and stitch them with the Redwood trace using the correlation id. There might be some fuzz when timestamps differ, but we show a confidence score for stitch quality.

[12:35] Evan: You mentioned the token-level timeline earlier — can we export that as JSON for offline analysis?

[12:43] Connor: Yes, export is available as JSON, and we also provide a CSV view for quick ingestion into spreadsheets.

[13:00] Aisha: We're worried about storing request logs with PII. Does Redwood offer redaction?

[13:09] Maya: Yes, we have automatic PII redaction rules and you can add custom redaction patterns. For Dedicated/Private customers you can choose never to persist raw prompts — only hashed metadata and diagnostics.

[13:30] Priya: For the planned pilot, we'd need KMS integration and HSM support for keys.

[13:38] Connor: We support KMS integrations and can integrate with customer-managed keys for Private deployments. HSM for on-prem is part of our enterprise package. We'll include details in the security doc.

[13:55] Tom: Can you show the request playback with cache warm vs cold toggle?

[14:05] Connor: Sure, toggling the cache state now. First cold — you can see a 420ms increase per token on average and total latency moves from 900ms to 1.6s. Now warm — it drops back. I'll annotate the screenshot and attach.

[14:38] Aisha: That delta is significant. Do you have guidance on batching vs latency tradeoffs?

[14:45] Maya: Yes — Redwood Optimize provides suggestions: per-route batching configurations, max batch sizes, and how it impacts p50/p95. We'll send the Optimize report for similar workloads.

[15:05] Evan: For benchmarking, we want the script to simulate our bursty windows and mix of short and long contexts.

[15:13] Connor: I'll include a sample Jason — sorry JSON-based script that lets you parameterize context length distribution, qps, and error injection.

[15:30] Aisha: Can the console surface feature flags for prompt templates? we want to see which template caused the mismatch.

[15:40] Connor: You can tag requests with a template id header and the console will group by template; we also have a 'prompt diff' view that highlights tokenization mismatches between versions.

[16:00] Tom: On fallback routing, do you provide SLA-backed latency if we choose Dedicated+fallback?

[16:10] Maya: Dedicated has an SLA for capacity and latency within committed pools. If you allow fallback to hosted, that route won't be SLA-backed unless you have a specific contract — we can discuss dedicated fallback SLAs in the enterprise addendum.

[16:35] Priya: Regarding audits, could you share a sample audit log format and retention options?

[16:44] Connor: We'll add a sample export: JSON lines with time, request id, route decision, model version, and redwood node id. Retention is configurable per account.

[17:05] Aisha: Are there hooks to integrate with our incident management flow? e.g. PagerDuty triggers when a baseline regresses?

[17:14] Connor: Yes — alerts can fire webhooks or integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, or email. You can set thresholds per-route or per-metric.

[17:35] Evan: We'd like to see a live run where you replay three failing traces with different cache states and show the console suggested remediation.

[17:45] Connor: Let's do that. I'm queuing three traces now. First trace playback shows cache eviction and suggests increasing per-route cache or switching to a larger context optimized kernel. Second trace suggests a prompt normalization (we show token diffs). Third suggests retry/backoff adjustments because the gateway timed out.

[18:30] Aisha: For the second suggested remediation, how do we automate a rollback if the candidate fix regresses?

[18:42] Connor: Canary configuration can include automatic rollback rules: if your quality metric (e.g., hallucination rate or top-1 probs) regresses by x% at p95, the system rolls back and notifies stakeholders.

[19:05] Tom: Do you version the models used in playbacks so we can reproduce results months later?

[19:12] Connor: Yes — playbacks reference pinned model snapshots and we keep binaries for a retention window. For long-term reproducibility we can arrange archival retention.

[19:35] Priya: Is there a way to fuzz test prompts to see edge cases?

[19:44] Connor: We have a prompt fuzz runner that injects adversarial tokens and reports mismatches. It's part of the Optimize suite.

[20:05] Maya: Quick pause — I want to flag the security deep dive. Priya, you'll want to talk to our security lead about KMS and SOC2 artifacts. We'll set that up.

[20:20] Priya: Yes please. Also need encryption-at-rest specifics for request logs.

[20:30] Connor: We'll attach the security pack.

[20:40] Evan: How long is the pilot you recommend? 2 weeks? 1 month?

[20:48] Maya: For request archaeology a 2–4 week pilot is common: first week import traces and configure, second week run playback and remediation, final week validate SLA/cost tradeoffs. We can tailor.

[21:10] Aisha: We'd like to make progress quickly — can you scope what we need to send to start?

[21:18] Connor: We need a sample of failing traces (3–10), your SLO definitions, a list of routes you want monitored, and a test API key for playback sampling.

[21:30] Maya: I'll email the checklist and the playbook deck after this call.

[21:40] Tom: Any limitations on model types for playback? e.g., large context LLMs or quantized variants?

[21:50] Connor: Playback supports the model catalog we serve, including quantized variants and long-context variants up to 64k tokens depending on model. For private models we'd need a model upload/workflow.

[22:10] Evan: Is there any noise in the stitch when you have multiple proxies? we have some legacy proxies that rewrite headers.

[22:19] Connor: Header rewriting can complicate stitch quality — we have heuristics and a manual mapping UI where you can tell the console which header to trust for correlation.

[22:40] Aisha: Let's talk about retention — how long do you keep request logs in hosted mode by default?

[22:50] Maya: By default 30 days for raw logs, longer for metrics. For enterprise we can bump retention and meet e-discovery needs.

[23:05] Priya: Do you support on-prem deployments for air-gapped scenarios?

[23:12] Connor: Yes, Redwood Private can be deployed on-prem; in that case the observability control plane sits in your environment. We have an on-prem packaging.

[23:30] Evan: Okay, last technical Q — can we run bulk request replays (e.g., 10k requests) without affecting production?

[23:39] Connor: Bulk replays run in sandbox capacity and are isolated from production; they can be throttled to control QPS. For large replays we typically recommend a dedicated sandbox pool.

[24:00] Maya: Wrapping up demo portion — we'll capture the three traces, Connor will attach the benchmark script and sample outputs, and we'll follow up with security docs.

[24:15] Aisha: Sounds good. Quick nit — when you export the audit CSV, can you include the original header name for correlation?

[24:25] Connor: Yes, we'll include the raw header fields in the audit export.

[24:40] Evan: Anything else on cost modeling?

[24:46] Maya: We'll include an example cost delta table: Hosted baseline vs Dedicated commit with fallback scenarios. We'll also show unit token cost and per-request amortized estimates.

[25:05] Tom: One last question — you mentioned AI model debug logs include per-layer timings. How intrusive is that on performance?

[25:15] Connor: The per-layer timing sampling is low overhead when enabled at low sampling rates; for full sampling we recommend sandbox runs. We default to lightweight telemetry in production to avoid perturbing latency.

[25:40] Priya: Thanks. We'll review and pick dates for the pilot.

[25:48] Maya: Great. I'll send the materials and calendar invites for the security deep-dive.

[26:00] (crosstalk)

[26:07] Connor: Quick note — some of the model names in your traces got normalized to Redwood model aliases; that can be toggled to show original upstream names if helpful.

[26:25] Aisha: Appreciate that.

[26:32] Evan: Onboarding time — how quickly can we stand up the instrumentation?

[26:39] Maya: For basic tracing it's a matter of dropping a small middleware and turning on correlation headers; typical time to instrument is a few days for an initial route. For more complex systems we'd estimate 1–2 weeks.

[26:58] Tom: Great. We'll aim to have the traces and SLO doc to you by Tuesday.

[27:05] Maya: Perfect. Anything else before we close?

[27:10] Priya: Nothing from security — just the deep dive scheduling.

[27:16] Aisha: No further questions. Thanks.

[27:20] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

Recap / Notes:
- Customer wants a 2–4 week pilot focusing on request archaeology for peak-window failures.
- Connor to provide benchmark script, cache toggle demo artifacts, and sample exports.
- Security team to get SOC2/KMS/HSM docs and schedule deep dive.
- Action items captured above.
